The longest shortest path runs from A to F in four hops (shown in the accent color along one of the two equal routes), so the diameter is 4." width="100%"} The diameter is the longest shortest path between any two nodes. This metric is useful for understanding the "width" of a network. It is computed by running a breadth-first search from every node to find its *eccentricity* (the distance to the farthest node it can reach) and taking the maximum. Distances are counted in hops, so edge weights are ignored, and in directed graphs paths must follow edge directions. The cost is one traversal per node, roughly `O(n * (n + m))`. The diameter is used to: - bound the worst-case number of steps a message or infection needs to reach everyone - compare the overall "size" of networks independently of their node counts - spot long chains or stringy appendages that stretch a network out A single long chain is enough to make the diameter large, so for a picture of typical separation, look at `mean_distance()` as well. `radius()` is its counterpart (the smallest eccentricity). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [unconnected]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Controls what happens when some nodes cannot reach each other. If `True` (default), each node's eccentricity only considers the nodes it can reach, so the result is the largest diameter among the connected components. If `False`, the method returns `None` unless every node can reach every other. For directed graphs this means strong connectivity, as in `mean_distance()`: a directed graph that is only weakly connected has unreachable pairs, so it returns `None`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Maximum distance between any two nodes, or `None` if disconnected (when `unconnected=False`). Also `None` for an empty graph. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a four-node path the farthest pair is A and D, three hops apart: ::: {#13359deb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D")]) ) graph.diameter() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: Closing the path into a cycle with an edge from D back to A brings every pair within two hops of each other: ::: {#981ad858 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.add_edge("D", "A") graph.diameter() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: For a disconnected graph the default reports the largest diameter among the components (here `2`, from the chain A-B-C, rather than the `1` of the pair D-E), while `unconnected=False` returns `None`: ::: {#271b1f4e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} split = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("D", "E")]) ) (split.diameter(), split.diameter(unconnected=False)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (2, None) ``` ::: :::
